lessons.title: Yalta and Potsdam: Allies Become Rivals
lessons.description: How the wartime alliance fractured at Yalta and Potsdam, and the seeds of postwar division.
lessons.content_html:
An Alliance Under Strain

By February 1945 the defeat of Nazi Germany was only weeks away. The Big Three — Joseph Stalin of the USSR, Franklin D. Roosevelt of the USA and Winston Churchill of Britain — met at the Crimean resort of Yalta to plan the peace. They had fought as allies for almost four years, but their interests had never truly aligned. Stalin wanted permanent security on his western border after losing perhaps 27 million Soviet citizens. Roosevelt wanted the USSR inside a new United Nations and willing to help finish the war against Japan. Churchill wanted to limit Soviet influence in Europe before the Red Army turned its conquest of Eastern Europe into political control.

Key Fact

The Yalta Conference ran from 4–11 February 1945 and the Potsdam Conference from 17 July to 2 August 1945. Roosevelt died in April 1945, so by Potsdam Truman had replaced him; Churchill lost the British general election mid-conference and was replaced by Clement Attlee.

What Yalta Agreed

Yalta produced a surprising amount of agreement on paper. Germany would be split into four zones of occupation, run by Britain, France, the USA and the USSR, with Berlin — deep inside the Soviet zone — also divided four ways. Nazi war criminals would be put on trial. The USSR pledged to enter the war against Japan within three months of Germany’s surrender, in return for territorial concessions in the Far East. The Big Three signed a Declaration on Liberated Europe promising free elections in the countries freed from Nazi rule.

The hardest issue was Poland. The USSR had already installed a friendly communist government, the Lublin Committee, while Polish exiles in London claimed legitimacy. The compromise was to broaden the Lublin government with a few non-communists and call it provisional, with elections to follow. Poland’s borders shifted west: it lost territory to the USSR but gained land from defeated Germany. Stalin viewed this as a permanent buffer; Churchill viewed it as a temporary arrangement that genuine elections would correct.

From Yalta to Potsdam: Mood Shift

Five months changed everything. Roosevelt died on 12 April 1945; his successor Harry S. Truman was less inclined to trust Stalin and more willing to confront him. Germany surrendered on 8 May. By the time the Big Three reconvened at Potsdam, just outside ruined Berlin, Soviet troops occupied most of Eastern Europe and showed no sign of leaving. On 16 July, the day before Potsdam opened, the USA secretly tested the world’s first atomic bomb in the New Mexico desert. Truman mentioned the existence of a powerful new weapon to Stalin in passing — Stalin, alerted by Soviet spies, was less surprised than Truman expected.

Britain held a general election on 5 July 1945, but the count was delayed for three weeks to allow servicemen’s votes to be returned. Churchill flew to Potsdam on 17 July believing he would still be Prime Minister when the conference closed. The result, declared on 26 July, was a Labour landslide. Churchill resigned the same day and Clement Attlee took his place at the negotiating table on 28 July. The change made little practical difference to British policy — Attlee had attended Yalta as deputy and broadly shared Churchill’s suspicion of Soviet intentions — but it underlined Stalin’s point that democracies were unstable allies.

What Potsdam Decided — and What It Did Not

Potsdam confirmed the four-zone occupation of Germany and Berlin. It set out the ‘Four Ds’ for occupied Germany: denazification, demilitarisation, democratisation and decentralisation. Reparations would be drawn from each occupier’s zone, with the Soviets allowed to take additional industrial equipment from the Western zones in exchange for food shipments from their agricultural east. The German-Polish border moved to the Oder-Neisse line, even though final borders were supposed to wait for a peace treaty.

Beneath the agreements, the disputes were sharper. Truman pressed for free elections across Eastern Europe under the Yalta declaration; Stalin replied that Soviet security required friendly governments and that the West had not held elections in liberated Italy. The atom bomb sharpened the gap. On 26 July the USA, Britain and Nationalist China issued the Potsdam Declaration demanding Japanese surrender; nine days after the conference closed, Hiroshima was destroyed. The Soviet entry into the war against Japan, agreed at Yalta as essential, suddenly looked optional.

Stalin demanded $20 billion in reparations from Germany, half for the USSR. Truman refused a fixed figure, remembering how the harsh reparations after 1919 had wrecked the Weimar economy. The Potsdam compromise — each occupier strips their own zone — looked workable but planted a seed of division. The Soviets took factories, livestock and machinery from the east; the West rebuilt the industrial Ruhr. Within two years the two halves of Germany were on visibly different economic paths, and the cross-zone food-for-equipment exchange had collapsed.

Why Historians Disagree About Origins

From the start, observers asked who turned the wartime alliance into Cold War rivalry. Some argue Stalin’s expansion in Eastern Europe was the cause; some argue Truman’s atom-bomb diplomacy was; some argue neither side ‘started’ it because the structures of the postwar world — two surviving great powers with opposed ideologies — made conflict almost certain. Examiners do not expect students to name these schools of thought, but the strongest answers recognise that Yalta and Potsdam can be read as the moment ideological differences crystallised into rival policies, rather than as a story with a single villain.

Key Fact

Potsdam confirmed the four-zone occupation, the ‘Four Ds’ policy and zone-based reparations, but exposed deep splits over free elections in Eastern Europe and the meaning of the new American atom bomb. The conference is often described as the moment the alliance turned into a rivalry that had not yet been named.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For an 8-mark Narrative Account on the breakdown of the wartime alliance, the examiner is looking for a chain of cause and consequence, not a list of meetings. Each event should connect to the next using phrases like ‘this in turn forced’, ‘because of this fear’ and ‘as a result’. Aim for three or four linked steps that span Yalta, Roosevelt’s death, the atom-bomb test and the Potsdam disputes — each step explaining why the next happened.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Yalta in February 1945 produced public agreement on dividing Germany, free elections in Eastern Europe and Soviet entry into the war against Japan, but glossed over fundamental disagreements about Poland.
  • Roosevelt’s death, the atom-bomb test and the visible Soviet hold on Eastern Europe meant Potsdam in July 1945 was a sharper, more suspicious meeting between leaders who no longer shared a common enemy.
  • The two conferences crystallised the structures of postwar Europe — the four zones of Germany, the Oder-Neisse border, the ‘Four Ds’ — while exposing the ideological gap that would harden into the Cold War.

practice_questions.text: Construct a chronological explanation of how the wartime alliance moved from agreement at Yalta in February 1945 to open disagreement at Potsdam in July–August 1945.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear analytical narrative linking three or more events as a chain of cause and consequence; uses precise factual detail (Yalta agreements, Roosevelt’s death, German surrender, Trinity test, Potsdam disputes); reaches Potsdam through a substantiated sequence.
Secure: A clear sequence of three or more linked events with some causal connectives and accurate detail.
Developing: Some relevant events listed in roughly the right order; causal links partial or implicit.
Emerging: A thin or muddled chronology with little linking between events.

Indicative content:
• February 1945: Yalta produced agreement on four-zone occupation, free elections in liberated Europe and Soviet entry into the war against Japan within three months of German surrender.
• April 1945: Roosevelt died and was replaced by Truman, who was more suspicious of Stalin’s intentions, narrowing the diplomatic warmth that had carried Yalta.
• May–July 1945: Germany surrendered on 8 May; Soviet troops occupied most of Eastern Europe and the promised elections did not materialise.
• 16 July 1945: the USA tested the first atomic bomb at Trinity, giving Truman a weapon that altered the balance of negotiation before Potsdam opened.
• 17 July–2 August 1945: Potsdam confirmed the ‘Four Ds’ for Germany and the Oder-Neisse border, but exposed deep splits over Eastern European elections and reparations.
• 26 July 1945: Attlee replaced Churchill mid-conference, signalling to Stalin the political instability of his western partners.

practice_questions.text: Construct a chronological explanation of how the disputes at Yalta and Potsdam shaped the future of Germany between February 1945 and August 1945.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative with three or more linked events showing causation; precise dates and details; arrives at the post-Potsdam shape of Germany through a substantiated chain.
Secure: Three or more linked events; some causal connectives; mostly accurate.
Developing: Events listed roughly in order; causal links partial.
Emerging: Thin chronology, weak linkage.

Indicative content:
• Yalta agreed Germany would be divided into four zones of occupation, with Berlin similarly divided though deep inside the Soviet zone.
• Yalta postponed reparations totals, leaving the issue to be resolved later.
• Germany’s surrender on 8 May 1945 brought Soviet, American, British and French troops into their respective zones, putting the Yalta plan into practice.
• Potsdam confirmed the four zones and added the ‘Four Ds’: denazification, demilitarisation, democratisation and decentralisation.
• Potsdam set the German-Polish border at the Oder-Neisse line, transferring large areas to Polish control.
• Reparations would now be taken zone-by-zone, with limited cross-zone exchange — a compromise that allowed each occupier to run its zone differently and prepared the ground for two German economies.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source A.

Source A: An extract from a memorandum by Charles ‘Chip’ Bohlen, the State Department’s Russian expert and Roosevelt’s interpreter at Yalta, written for internal US use shortly after the conference in February 1945.
‘The Marshal speaks of friendly governments along his frontier in the same breath that he signs a declaration promising free elections. We must accept that these two ideas, in his mind, are not in conflict; in ours, they cannot both be honoured. The Polish question is therefore the test of whether the alliance can survive the peace.’

Using Source A, identify two reasons Bohlen gives for thinking the Polish settlement at Yalta was unstable.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies two clearly distinct reasons drawn precisely from the source, supported by short embedded references.
Secure: Identifies two relevant reasons from the source, with brief support.
Developing: Identifies one clear reason; second point vague or repeats the first.
Emerging: General comment about the source without identifying specific reasons.

Indicative content:
• Stalin treats ‘friendly governments’ as compatible with free elections, while the Americans see the two as contradictory.
• Stalin signed the Declaration on Liberated Europe but is already attaching a security condition to it.
• Bohlen argues the two ideas cannot both be honoured at the same time.
• The Polish question is described as the ‘test’ of the alliance, implying its failure would unravel cooperation.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source B and Source C.

Source B: An extract from Stalin’s remarks at Yalta on 6 February 1945, recorded in the official British minute of the plenary sessions.
‘For Russia, the question of Poland is not only one of honour, but one of security. Twice in thirty years, Germany has invaded Russia through the Polish corridor. We need governments to our west which are loyal, not hostile. The Soviet Union cannot accept any other solution.’

Source C: An extract from Truman’s diary entry of 17 July 1945, the first day of the Potsdam Conference.
‘Stalin came in to see me before the meeting. He is a hard-headed bargainer; one must give to get. He wants Eastern Europe; we want Japan and a stable Germany. The atomic test in New Mexico has changed the picture in ways he cannot yet see.’

Evaluate the usefulness of Sources B and C to a historian studying the breakdown of cooperation between the wartime allies in 1945. Use the sources and your knowledge of the period in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of both sources weighing content, provenance and contextual knowledge; reaches a substantiated judgement on the usefulness of each.
Secure: Clear evaluation of both sources using all three elements (content, provenance, knowledge); judgement made.
Developing: Some evaluation, but tends to handle two of the three elements rather than all three; judgement may be implicit.
Emerging: Describes the sources or comments on bias only; little integration of own knowledge.

Indicative content:
Source B — Content: Stalin frames Poland as a Soviet security issue, citing twice-invaded territory. Provenance: an official British minute of Stalin’s own words at Yalta — close to a primary record of his stated position, though shaped for an Allied audience. Own knowledge: Operation Barbarossa in 1941 had left perhaps 27 million Soviet dead; the Soviet demand for ‘friendly’ governments was rooted in this trauma.
Source C — Content: Truman casts Stalin as transactional and the atom bomb as a quiet game-changer. Provenance: a private diary on the day of a major meeting — useful for capturing immediate impressions but coloured by Truman’s own self-image. Own knowledge: the Trinity test had occurred the day before; Truman would mention the bomb to Stalin on 24 July, though Stalin already knew through Soviet intelligence.
Judgement: Both are useful but partial — B reveals Soviet logic in Stalin’s own words, C reveals American instincts at the moment Potsdam began — together they show why the alliance frayed before either side took an obviously hostile step.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source D and Source E.

Source D: An extract from Churchill’s telegram to Truman, sent on 12 May 1945, four days after Germany’s surrender, drawn from the Churchill Papers held at Cambridge.
‘An iron curtain is drawn down upon their front. We do not know what is going on behind. There is little doubt that the whole of the regions east of the line Lubeck-Trieste-Corfu will soon be in their hands. We must reach a settlement with Russia before our armies melt away.’

Source E: An extract from a 1948 article by the American journalist Walter Lippmann, looking back on the Potsdam Conference.
‘Potsdam was the conference at which the wartime alliance ended without ever being formally dissolved. The leaders shook hands and signed a communiqué, but they had stopped pretending that they shared the same vision of Europe.’

Write an essay on the question: ‘The personal change of leadership between Yalta and Potsdam was the main reason the wartime alliance broke down by August 1945.’ Using Sources D and E and your own knowledge, evaluate the claim.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained argument addressing the specific claim; integrates content, provenance and own knowledge from both sources; reaches a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with relevant use of both sources; judgement reached and supported.
Developing: Some argument with reference to both sources, but use of provenance or own knowledge limited; judgement may be partial.
Emerging: Describes the sources or covers events without engaging with the specific claim.

Indicative content:
Supporting the claim:
• Roosevelt’s death and replacement by Truman shifted the American line from accommodation to suspicion within weeks.
• Churchill’s replacement by Attlee on 28 July introduced a new British voice into Potsdam mid-flow.
• Source E describes the alliance ending without being formally dissolved — consistent with leadership change rather than a single rupture.

Challenging the claim:
• Source D shows Churchill himself recognising the ‘iron curtain’ before Roosevelt died — the structural problem was already visible.
• Soviet behaviour in Poland — ignoring the Yalta declaration on free elections — would have produced friction whoever sat in the White House.
• The atom bomb gave Truman a new card; even with Roosevelt the bomb would still have arrived at Potsdam.
• Reparations and the meaning of ‘friendly’ governments were structural disputes that pre-dated the leadership change.

Judgement: leadership change accelerated the breakdown but did not cause it — the structural disagreements identified in Source D were already pulling the alliance apart by spring 1945.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source F.

Source F: An extract from a private letter from Clement Attlee to his brother Tom, written shortly after returning from Potsdam in early August 1945.
‘The Russians are tough negotiators but not unreasonable on detail. The trouble is that we cannot agree on the larger picture. They believe we are scheming to rebuild Germany against them; we believe they are scheming to make Eastern Europe communist. Both, I fear, are partly right.’

Identify two ways in which Source F is useful to a historian studying mutual suspicion at the Potsdam Conference.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly developed points using content and provenance, reinforced by precise own knowledge.
Secure: Two clear points; uses content and either provenance or own knowledge; some development.
Developing: Two points but undeveloped, or one point fully and one weakly.
Emerging: One general point or surface description.

Indicative content:
• Content: Source F captures the symmetry of suspicion — each side believes the other is scheming — useful evidence that mistrust at Potsdam was mutual rather than one-sided.
• Content: Attlee’s admission that ‘both are partly right’ reveals a leader who can see his own side’s contribution to the breakdown.
• Provenance: A private letter to a family member, written immediately after the conference, is likely to capture genuine views with less diplomatic varnish than a public statement.
• Own knowledge: This matches the historical record — the West did move toward rebuilding the Western zones of Germany, while the USSR did consolidate communist parties across Eastern Europe.
• Limitation worth noting: a single private letter cannot represent the full British cabinet view, and Attlee may have been managing his brother’s anxieties as much as analysing the conference.

lessons.title: The Atom Bomb, Ideologies, and the Iron Curtain
lessons.description: How the atom bomb, rival ideologies and Soviet expansion produced Churchill's Iron Curtain warning.
lessons.content_html:
Two Visions of the Postwar World

By 1945 the wartime alliance held two fundamentally different ideas of how society should be run. The USA championed capitalism and liberal democracy: free elections, multi-party politics, freedom of the press, and an economy of competing private businesses. The USSR championed communism: a single-party state under the Communist Party, a planned economy with state-owned industry, and the ideological goal of spreading revolution to other countries. The two systems were not just different policies; each treated the other as a threat to its survival.

Key Fact

By 1945 the USA and USSR were the two surviving superpowers, but their ideologies were opposites. Americans feared communism would spread by force into a war-shattered Europe; Soviets feared capitalism would encircle them with hostile neighbours, just as Germany had done in 1941.

The Atom Bomb Changes the Equation

On 6 August 1945 a single American B-29 dropped an atom bomb on Hiroshima; three days later Nagasaki was destroyed in the same way. Around 200,000 Japanese civilians were killed, most of them in the immediate blast. Japan surrendered on 15 August. The military effect was decisive, but the political effect on the wartime alliance was just as great. The Soviets had broken into the war against Japan only on 9 August. Their reward at Yalta — territorial concessions in the Far East — suddenly mattered less, because Truman had a weapon that did not need a Soviet front.

Stalin understood almost immediately that a US monopoly on atomic weapons threatened Soviet security. He had known about the Manhattan Project through Soviet espionage and now ordered Soviet scientists to match it. Through the rest of the 1940s, the bomb sat between the two former allies as both a deterrent and a provocation. Some historians describe Truman’s use of the bomb as the first move of the Cold War; others argue it was simply the last act of the Second World War. The truth is probably both: the same explosion ended one war and helped start another.

On 24 July 1945 Truman casually told Stalin that the USA had a ‘new weapon of unusual destructive force’. Truman was watching for a reaction; Stalin barely showed one. The reason became clear later: Soviet intelligence had penetrated the Manhattan Project years earlier, and Stalin already knew the bomb existed. Some scholars argue Truman timed the news of the Trinity test to harden his negotiating line at Potsdam. Others point out he had little practical choice once the test succeeded. Either way, when Hiroshima was destroyed two weeks after Potsdam closed, Stalin saw it not just as the end of Japan but as a message to him.

Soviet Expansion in Eastern Europe

By the end of 1945 the Red Army occupied Poland, Hungary, Romania, Bulgaria, eastern Germany and parts of Czechoslovakia and Austria. Stalin had pledged at Yalta to allow free elections in liberated countries, but the elections that took place between 1945 and 1948 were rigged or manipulated to bring local communist parties to power. Non-communist politicians were arrested, exiled or executed. By early 1948 every Soviet-occupied state was run by a single-party communist government loyal to Moscow. Stalin called this a ‘belt of friendly states’; Churchill and Truman called it conquest by stealth.

The pattern varied country by country. In Poland the rigged 1947 election confirmed the communist hold already in place. In Hungary, communists who had won only 17 per cent of the vote in 1945 used ‘salami tactics’ — slicing off rival parties one at a time — to take over by 1948. In Czechoslovakia, where communists were genuinely popular, a non-violent coup in February 1948 finished the job. The pattern was unmistakable, and the Yalta promise of free elections was, in practice, dead.

Churchill’s Iron Curtain Speech

On 5 March 1946 Winston Churchill, no longer Prime Minister, spoke at Westminster College in Fulton, Missouri, with President Truman in the audience. He warned that ‘from Stettin in the Baltic to Trieste in the Adriatic, an iron curtain has descended across the Continent’. The phrase was not new — Churchill had used ‘iron curtain’ in his May 1945 telegram to Truman — but Fulton turned it into a public diagnosis. Behind the Iron Curtain, he argued, lay capitals under Soviet influence; Soviet ambitions were not for war but for ‘the indefinite expansion of their power and doctrines’.

In the USA the speech was controversial: many Americans still hoped to keep working with the USSR, and some newspapers accused Churchill of warmongering. Truman, to keep his options open, publicly distanced himself from the speech even though he had read it in advance. In Moscow, Stalin compared Churchill’s argument to Hitler’s rhetoric on racial superiority, declaring that the Soviet sphere was a defensive necessity, not a programme for conquest. Within a year, however, US policy had shifted in Churchill’s direction: the Truman Doctrine of March 1947 echoed the Fulton diagnosis almost word for word.

A Rivalry Without a Name

By the end of 1946 the language of partnership was gone. Truman’s officials in Moscow, including the diplomat George Kennan, sent home long memos arguing that the USSR understood only firmness. Stalin’s officials briefed the Politburo that capitalist encirclement was the new strategic reality. Public opinion in both countries was beginning to catch up. The phrase ‘Cold War’ would not be coined until 1947, but the pattern was already set: an ideological rivalry, sharpened by the bomb, mapped onto a divided Europe.

Key Fact

Churchill’s ‘Iron Curtain’ speech at Fulton, Missouri on 5 March 1946 named the divide running from Stettin in the Baltic to Trieste in the Adriatic. It did not start the Cold War — the elections in Eastern Europe had already been rigged — but it gave the public a vocabulary for what was happening.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For a 4-mark Source Analysis on the early Cold War, read the source twice before you start writing. Identify two clearly distinct points the source actually makes, and quote a short phrase to support each. The examiner is testing inference, not your wider knowledge — so do not bring in extra information. Keep both points specific and tied to the source’s wording.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • American capitalism and Soviet communism were opposing systems by 1945, and each side feared the other’s ideology would spread by force or by example.
  • The atom bomb dropped on Hiroshima and Nagasaki ended the Second World War and gave the USA a temporary monopoly that reshaped its negotiations with Stalin.
  • Stalin’s rigged elections in Eastern Europe between 1945 and 1948 turned the Yalta promise of free elections into a divided continent — the ‘Iron Curtain’ that Churchill named at Fulton in March 1946.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source A.

Source A: An extract from Winston Churchill’s ‘Sinews of Peace’ speech at Westminster College, Fulton, Missouri, 5 March 1946.
‘From Stettin in the Baltic to Trieste in the Adriatic, an iron curtain has descended across the Continent. Behind that line lie all the capitals of the ancient states of Central and Eastern Europe… all are subject, in one form or another, not only to Soviet influence but to a very high and increasing measure of control from Moscow.’

Using Source A, identify two reasons Churchill gives for being concerned about Soviet behaviour in Europe.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies two clearly distinct reasons drawn precisely from the source, supported by short embedded references.
Secure: Identifies two relevant reasons from the source, with brief support.
Developing: Identifies one clear reason; second point vague or repeats the first.
Emerging: General comment about the source without identifying specific reasons.

Indicative content:
• An ‘iron curtain’ has descended — Europe is now divided.
• Capitals of Central and Eastern Europe lie behind that line — the divide includes major historical cities.
• Those countries are subject to Soviet influence and growing Moscow control.
• The ‘increasing measure of control’ phrase implies that Soviet domination is deepening, not stable.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source B.

Source B: An extract from a State Department telegram from George Kennan, US chargé d’affaires in Moscow, sent on 22 February 1946 and known later as the ‘Long Telegram’.
‘The Soviet view is that there can be no permanent peaceful coexistence with capitalism. The USSR will press at every weak point until it meets resistance. We must build economic strength in our partners abroad and self-confidence at home, for force is the only language they respect.’

Using Source B, identify two arguments Kennan makes about how the USA should respond to the USSR.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies two clearly distinct arguments drawn precisely from the source, supported by short embedded references.
Secure: Identifies two relevant arguments from the source, with brief support.
Developing: Identifies one clear argument; second point vague or repeats the first.
Emerging: General comment about the source without identifying specific arguments.

Indicative content:
• Build economic strength in partners abroad.
• Build self-confidence at home.
• Recognise that the USSR sees no permanent peaceful coexistence with capitalism.
• Use force as the ‘only language they respect’ — meet pressure with resistance.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source C and Source D.

Source C: An extract from a 1947 Soviet government statement on the Iron Curtain Speech, broadcast by Moscow Radio in March 1946.
‘Mr Churchill calls for a war of nerves against the peace-loving peoples of Eastern Europe. He forgets that the USSR lost twenty-seven million dead defending those same peoples from fascism. Our friendship with our western neighbours is not control; it is the natural product of shared sacrifice.’

Source D: An extract from a private letter from US Secretary of State James Byrnes to a Senator, written in April 1946.
‘The Russian elections in Poland and Romania have been a humiliating spectacle. Our protests through diplomatic channels have produced nothing. The patient policy of the past twelve months is at an end; we shall now speak more plainly.’

Evaluate the usefulness of Sources C and D to a historian studying the breakdown of cooperation between the USA and USSR in 1946. Use the sources and your knowledge of the period in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of both sources weighing content, provenance and contextual knowledge; reaches a substantiated judgement on the usefulness of each.
Secure: Clear evaluation of both sources using all three elements (content, provenance, knowledge); judgement made.
Developing: Some evaluation, but tends to handle two of the three elements rather than all three; judgement may be implicit.
Emerging: Describes the sources or comments on bias only; little integration of own knowledge.

Indicative content:
Source C — Content: rejects Churchill’s argument and frames Soviet influence as ‘natural friendship’. Provenance: an official Soviet broadcast in 1946, designed to shape domestic and international opinion — useful for revealing the public Soviet line, less useful for revealing private Soviet calculation. Own knowledge: Soviet wartime losses were genuine and shaped the demand for friendly western neighbours, but the rigged elections in Poland and Hungary contradict the ‘natural friendship’ framing.
Source D — Content: announces a tougher US line after twelve months of patience. Provenance: a private letter from the Secretary of State to a Senator in 1946 — close to the inner US discussion, candid in tone, useful for capturing the moment policy shifted. Own knowledge: the Truman Doctrine was less than a year away; Byrnes’s frustration matches Kennan’s ‘Long Telegram’ arguments from February 1946.
Judgement: Both are useful but partial — together they show how each side framed the breakdown for a domestic audience while privately recognising the structural problem.

lessons.title: Truman Doctrine and Marshall Plan
lessons.description: How the Truman Doctrine and Marshall Plan turned containment into policy and split Europe in two.
lessons.content_html:
The Crisis That Pushed Truman to Speak

By February 1947 the British government was bankrupt. Coal shortages, a brutal winter and the cost of empire meant Britain could no longer fund the Greek government in its civil war against communist guerrillas, or maintain the British military presence in Turkey. On 21 February the British ambassador delivered a blunt note in Washington: from 31 March, support for Greece and Turkey would end. Officials in the State Department recognised the moment immediately. If Greece fell to the communists, Turkey would be next; if Turkey fell, the Soviet navy would have access to the Mediterranean and oil-rich states beyond.

Key Fact

Truman announced his doctrine to Congress on 12 March 1947. It was triggered by Britain’s February note that it could no longer support Greece and Turkey, and it framed US foreign policy around the choice between ‘two ways of life’: democracy and free institutions, or oppression and control.

The Truman Doctrine

In his speech to Congress on 12 March 1947, Truman asked for $400 million of military and economic aid for Greece and Turkey. The numbers mattered, but the language mattered more. Truman declared: ‘It must be the policy of the United States to support free peoples who are resisting attempted subjugation by armed minorities or by outside pressures.’ This was a permanent commitment, known as the Truman Doctrine, to oppose the spread of communism wherever it appeared. Inside the US government, this approach was already known by a name: containment.

Containment did not aim to roll back Soviet power in countries already controlled by Moscow. The point was to draw a line. Where the line ran would be tested over the next four decades, but Greece and Turkey were the first two stones in the wall. By the end of 1949, with US aid and reorganised forces, Greek government troops had defeated the communist guerrillas. Turkey had stabilised. The doctrine had passed its first test.

George Kennan’s Long Telegram in February 1946, and his July 1947 article in Foreign Affairs signed ‘X’, supplied the intellectual case for containment. Kennan argued that the USSR was driven by an internal need for hostile encirclement and would back down only when met with ‘long-term, patient but firm and vigilant containment’. Truman’s speechwriters borrowed the framing but stripped out Kennan’s reservations. Kennan himself later complained that his policy had been globalised into a crusade he had not intended — a useful warning that policies and the speeches that announce them are not always the same thing.

From Doctrine to Dollars: The Marshall Plan

Three months after the Truman speech, US Secretary of State George Marshall stood at Harvard on 5 June 1947 and offered something more ambitious. Europe’s economies were broken. Hunger and unemployment, Marshall argued, were a breeding ground for political extremism. The USA would provide large-scale economic aid to any European country that asked — on condition that the recipients meet together to plan how to use it. The Marshall Plan ran from 1948 to 1952 and delivered roughly $13 billion to sixteen European countries.

Marshall was careful at Harvard to extend the offer to the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe. Stalin understood the trap. Accepting Marshall aid would mean opening Soviet economies to American inspection, attaching Eastern Europe to a US-led programme and undermining the case for Soviet protection. He refused, and forbade Czechoslovakia and Poland — both of which had begun to negotiate — from accepting either. The plan therefore did exactly what its critics in Moscow expected: it tied the recipients to the West and divided Europe in two.

Why It Worked — and Why Stalin Saw a Threat

Marshall aid was political as well as economic. The money rebuilt Western European industry, restored trade between countries that had spent six years at war, and gave moderate parties in France and Italy something concrete to point to against rising communist parties. By 1952 industrial output in the recipient countries was about a third higher than before the war. The plan also paid for the Allied zones of Germany to recover, which Stalin read as the rebuilding of a future enemy.

From the Soviet view, the plan was ‘dollar imperialism’: the USA buying influence with money the USSR could not match. The Soviet response, Cominform, would follow in September 1947 (covered in the next lesson), but the deeper damage was that the door of cooperation closed. After Marshall, the wartime alliance was no longer just strained — it had been replaced by a system in which each side built parallel institutions for its own bloc.

The phrase ‘two ways of life’ became central to American Cold War thinking. Truman insisted that economic aid would not work without political confidence: hungry people in 1947 did not believe in democracy because it tasted like freedom; they believed in whichever system kept them fed. The Marshall Plan was therefore not separate from the Truman Doctrine but its economic engine. Together they framed the USA as the protector of a free Western system while making any country that accepted the dollars a partner in that system, not a neutral bystander.

Key Fact

The Marshall Plan was announced by George C. Marshall at Harvard on 5 June 1947 and ran from 1948 to 1952. It delivered around $13 billion to sixteen Western European countries. Stalin refused it for the USSR and forbade Eastern European states from accepting, deepening the split between the two halves of Europe.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For a 12-mark Source Evaluation question, the examiner is looking for content, provenance and own knowledge across both sources. A common mistake is to do two of the three for both sources rather than all three. Plan briefly: for each source note one piece of useful content, one provenance point (who, when, why), and one fact from your own knowledge that supports or qualifies it — then weigh both together in a clear judgement.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Truman Doctrine of 12 March 1947 turned the containment of communism into permanent US policy, triggered by the British inability to keep funding Greece and Turkey.
  • The Marshall Plan, announced at Harvard on 5 June 1947 and running until 1952, delivered around $13 billion to sixteen Western European countries and tied their recovery to the USA.
  • Stalin’s refusal to allow Eastern European states to accept Marshall aid converted what could have been a Europe-wide programme into a wedge that split the continent into two economic blocs.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source A.

Source A: An extract from President Harry Truman’s speech to a joint session of Congress, 12 March 1947, asking for aid to Greece and Turkey.
‘At the present moment in world history nearly every nation must choose between alternative ways of life… One way of life is based upon the will of the majority and is distinguished by free institutions, representative government, free elections… The second way of life is based upon the will of a minority forcibly imposed upon the majority. It relies upon terror and oppression, a controlled press and radio, fixed elections, and the suppression of personal freedoms.’

Using Source A, identify two reasons Truman gives for asking Congress to support free peoples abroad.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies two clearly distinct reasons drawn precisely from the source, supported by short embedded references.
Secure: Identifies two relevant reasons from the source, with brief support.
Developing: Identifies one clear reason; second point vague or repeats the first.
Emerging: General comment about the source without identifying specific reasons.

Indicative content:
• Free institutions and representative government depend on majority will and need protection.
• The alternative is rule by a minority based on terror, oppression and fixed elections.
• A controlled press and radio show how the second way of life suppresses personal freedoms.
• ‘Nearly every nation must choose’ implies a global stake, not just a Greek-Turkish problem.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source B and Source C.

Source B: An extract from George Marshall’s speech at Harvard University, 5 June 1947, announcing what became the Marshall Plan.
‘Our policy is directed not against any country or doctrine but against hunger, poverty, desperation and chaos. Its purpose should be the revival of a working economy in the world so as to permit the emergence of political and social conditions in which free institutions can exist.’

Source C: An extract from Foreign Minister Vyacheslav Molotov’s statement to the Paris Conference, 2 July 1947, walking out of talks on the Marshall Plan.
‘The American proposal is not aid — it is a programme of conditions. We are asked to disclose our economic plans, accept American supervision and bind ourselves to a Western bloc. The Soviet government will have nothing to do with such a scheme.’

Evaluate the usefulness of Sources B and C to a historian studying why the Marshall Plan divided Europe in 1947. Use the sources and your knowledge of the period in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of both sources weighing content, provenance and contextual knowledge; reaches a substantiated judgement on the usefulness of each.
Secure: Clear evaluation of both sources using all three elements (content, provenance, knowledge); judgement made.
Developing: Some evaluation, but tends to handle two of the three elements rather than all three; judgement may be implicit.
Emerging: Describes the sources or comments on bias only; little integration of own knowledge.

Indicative content:
Source B — Content: presents Marshall’s offer as humanitarian, aimed at hunger and poverty rather than at the USSR. Provenance: a public Harvard speech by the US Secretary of State; useful for the official US framing, less useful as a guide to the political calculation behind the offer. Own knowledge: in private the State Department understood that economic aid would also strengthen pro-Western governments in France and Italy; the offer was crafted to be unacceptable to Stalin without being publicly directed at him.
Source C — Content: rejects the plan as an instrument of American supervision. Provenance: an official Soviet statement at the Paris Conference, designed for the public record — useful for the Soviet line, partial because it does not reveal the internal Soviet decision to forbid Czechoslovakia and Poland from accepting.
Own knowledge: by July 1947 Stalin had blocked both Czechoslovakian and Polish negotiation with the plan; sixteen Western European states received aid from 1948 to 1952; Cominform followed in September 1947.
Judgement: Both sources are useful but partial — B reveals the public US framing, C reveals the public Soviet line; together they show how the plan’s conditions, not just its money, made acceptance impossible for Stalin and so divided Europe.

Source E: An extract from a Pravda editorial, 16 June 1947, responding to the Harvard speech.
‘Mr Marshall’s speech is the second instalment of the Truman Doctrine, dressed in the kindlier clothing of bread and machinery. The dollar offered comes wrapped in the demand for economic surveillance and political loyalty. The peoples of Europe will not exchange one occupation for another.’

lessons.title: Stalin's Response: Cominform, Comecon and Yugoslavia
lessons.description: How Stalin tightened control through Cominform and Comecon, and why Tito's Yugoslavia broke away.
lessons.content_html:
Stalin’s Counter-Move

By summer 1947 the Marshall Plan had been announced, Eastern European communists had been forbidden to accept it, and the Truman Doctrine had given Western policy a name. Stalin needed a structure of his own. The next two years would see the creation of two parallel institutions — one political, one economic — and a public quarrel with the only Eastern European leader who refused to accept Soviet dictation: Yugoslavia’s Josip Broz Tito.

Key Fact

Cominform was founded at a secret meeting of nine European communist parties in Szklarska Poreba, Poland, in September 1947. It was first headquartered in Belgrade, Yugoslavia — until Yugoslavia was expelled in June 1948, after which the headquarters moved to Bucharest, Romania.

Cominform: Coordinating the Bloc

The Cominform was Stalin’s answer to the political logic of the Marshall Plan. Its founding meeting brought together communist parties from the USSR, Poland, Czechoslovakia, Hungary, Romania, Bulgaria, Yugoslavia, France and Italy. The Soviet representative Andrei Zhdanov delivered a speech announcing the ‘two camps’ doctrine: the world was now divided between an imperialist camp led by the USA and an anti-imperialist camp led by the USSR. There was no neutral middle ground.

In practice Cominform did three things. It coordinated propaganda, ensuring that communist parties across Europe attacked the Marshall Plan in similar terms. It enforced ideological discipline, demanding that any deviation from the Soviet line be denounced. And it told local parties when to obstruct, strike, or stand for office. The French and Italian communist parties had been part of postwar coalition governments; in 1947 they were ordered into opposition. Industrial unrest in France through the autumn of 1947 followed directly from Cominform decisions.

Zhdanov’s September 1947 speech is the clearest Soviet statement of how Stalin saw the Cold War. The world had two camps, the speech argued, and no third option was available. Countries that thought they were neutral were really clients of one camp or the other. The doctrine was useful to Stalin because it justified treating any independence inside Eastern Europe as defection. Yugoslavia would be its first victim, but the same logic later attacked Hungarian and Czechoslovak reformers. The doctrine also borrowed the language of Truman’s ‘two ways of life’, turning it into mirror image — both leaders, by 1947, were arguing that the world had to choose.

Comecon: The Economic Counter-Plan

Cominform handled politics; the economy needed its own response. In January 1949 Stalin announced Comecon — the Council for Mutual Economic Assistance. The founding members were the USSR, Poland, Czechoslovakia, Hungary, Romania and Bulgaria, with Albania joining within weeks and East Germany in 1950. On paper Comecon was a system of mutual aid; in reality the USSR set the prices, decided which country produced what, and channelled raw materials toward Soviet industrial priorities.

Comecon never delivered the kind of recovery the Marshall Plan generated. The Soviet economy did not have $13 billion to give away, and the rules of trade favoured the USSR. Eastern European countries were obliged to sell goods to Moscow at prices below world rates and to buy Soviet goods at prices above. Specialisation was decided in Moscow: Bulgaria grew tomatoes, Hungary built buses, East Germany made chemicals. The economic gap between Western and Eastern Europe, already visible by 1949, widened steadily through the 1950s.

Yugoslavia Breaks Away

Yugoslavia did not fit the pattern. The Yugoslav communists, led by Josip Broz Tito, had liberated their own country from Nazi occupation in 1944–45 with little Soviet help. Tito ran Yugoslavia as a one-party state but on Yugoslav terms, not Soviet ones. He pursued an independent foreign policy in the Balkans, signed treaties without consulting Moscow, and considered a Balkan federation with Bulgaria. Stalin saw all of this as insubordination. Letters between Stalin and Tito in the spring of 1948 escalated into a full quarrel; in June 1948, Cominform expelled Yugoslavia.

Tito did not collapse. The Yugoslav army was loyal, the Yugoslav party purged its pro-Soviet members rather than the other way round, and Tito turned to the West for emergency aid. By 1949 the USA was quietly supplying Yugoslavia with food and credits — an awkward partnership of capitalist and communist against Stalin. The Tito-Stalin split showed the limits of Soviet control: where local communists had genuine domestic legitimacy, Stalin could not unseat them. Across the bloc, however, the lesson Stalin drew was the opposite — that he must purge any leader showing ‘Titoist’ tendencies, which set off show trials in Hungary, Bulgaria and Czechoslovakia between 1949 and 1952.

The Yugoslav split punctured the image of a single, monolithic communist bloc. It also gave Western policymakers a useful test case. If Tito could be a communist outside the Soviet system, perhaps other Eastern European leaders could too. The encouragement of ‘national communism’ would feature in later Western thinking, including over Hungary in 1956. Stalin’s response was to tighten control, replacing the kind of patriotic communist who might think like Tito with party officials chosen for personal loyalty to Moscow.

Key Fact

By 1949 Stalin had built a parallel system: Cominform (1947) coordinated communist parties politically and Comecon (1949) tied Eastern European economies to the USSR. Yugoslavia’s expulsion in June 1948 showed that the system had limits, and triggered a wave of show trials across Eastern Europe to remove anyone who might think like Tito.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For an 8-mark Narrative Account, the examiner is looking for causal connections, not a list of dates. Pick three or four events that drove the next one, and use connectives like ‘this prompted’, ‘in turn’, ‘because of this’. For Stalin’s response to the Marshall Plan, a strong chain runs Marshall offer → Cominform → Tito split → Comecon and the show trials — each step pushing toward greater Soviet control of the bloc.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Cominform, founded in September 1947, coordinated communist parties across Europe behind a Soviet line and announced the ‘two camps’ doctrine that mirrored Truman’s ‘two ways of life’.
  • Comecon, founded in January 1949, tied Eastern European economies to Soviet planning, but never matched the Marshall Plan’s scale and widened the East-West economic gap.
  • Yugoslavia’s expulsion from Cominform in June 1948 showed the limits of Soviet control where local leaders had genuine legitimacy, and triggered Stalinist purges across the rest of Eastern Europe.

• April–May 1948: a series of letters between Stalin and Tito escalated into a public quarrel.
• 28 June 1948: Cominform expelled Yugoslavia; the headquarters moved to Bucharest.
• 1949: the USA began quietly providing food and credits to Yugoslavia, despite its communist government — a sign that the split had become permanent.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source A.

Source A: An extract from Andrei Zhdanov’s speech to the founding meeting of Cominform, Szklarska Poreba, September 1947.
‘The world is divided into two camps. On the one hand stands the imperialist camp led by the United States, dedicated to the enslavement of nations and the suppression of democracy. On the other stands the anti-imperialist camp led by the Soviet Union, dedicated to the cause of peace, sovereignty and democracy. Between them there is no neutral ground.’

Using Source A, identify two reasons Zhdanov gives for arguing that the world is divided into two opposing camps.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies two clearly distinct reasons drawn precisely from the source, supported by short embedded references.
Secure: Identifies two relevant reasons from the source, with brief support.
Developing: Identifies one clear reason; second point vague or repeats the first.
Emerging: General comment about the source without identifying specific reasons.

Indicative content:
• An imperialist camp led by the USA is dedicated to the ‘enslavement of nations’.
• An anti-imperialist camp led by the USSR is dedicated to peace, sovereignty and democracy.
• Each camp has fundamentally opposed aims, with no shared ground.
• Between the two camps there is no ‘neutral ground’, ruling out a third path.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source B and Source C.

Source B: An extract from a Cominform resolution expelling Yugoslavia, Bucharest, 28 June 1948.
‘The Yugoslav leaders have departed from the path of socialism, conducted a policy of slander against the Soviet Union, and refused to acknowledge the leading role of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union. Their party has placed itself outside the family of fraternal parties.’

Source C: An extract from Tito’s reply to the Cominform resolution, broadcast on Yugoslav radio in early July 1948.
‘We have not departed from the cause of socialism. We have refused only to be told by foreign comrades how to run our own country. The Yugoslav road is independent, but it is not anti-socialist. The accusation that we are agents of imperialism is an insult to the Yugoslav people who freed themselves with their own hands.’

Evaluate the usefulness of Sources B and C to a historian studying the Tito-Stalin split in 1948. Use the sources and your knowledge of the period in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of both sources weighing content, provenance and contextual knowledge; reaches a substantiated judgement on the usefulness of each.
Secure: Clear evaluation of both sources using all three elements (content, provenance, knowledge); judgement made.
Developing: Some evaluation, but tends to handle two of the three elements rather than all three; judgement may be implicit.
Emerging: Describes the sources or comments on bias only; little integration of own knowledge.

Indicative content:
Source B — Content: frames Yugoslavia as having abandoned socialism and rejected Soviet leadership. Provenance: an official Cominform document, designed to justify the expulsion to other parties — useful for the public Soviet line, less useful for the private grievances Stalin held. Own knowledge: the real disputes were over Tito’s independent foreign policy in the Balkans, not over socialist principle.
Source C — Content: rejects the accusation of departing from socialism, frames the dispute as one of independence rather than ideology. Provenance: Tito’s public broadcast, addressed to a Yugoslav audience that needed reassurance — useful for the line Tito wanted heard, partial because it cannot show the internal Yugoslav debate.
Own knowledge: the Yugoslav army and party stood with Tito; the USA began supplying food and credits in 1949; show trials in Hungary, Bulgaria and Czechoslovakia followed in 1949–52, removing leaders accused of Titoism.
Judgement: Both are useful but partial — B reveals how Cominform justified the expulsion to the bloc, C reveals how Tito framed it for his own people; together they show why neither side could back down.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source D.

Source D: An extract from a US National Security Council report on Yugoslavia, NSC 18, June 1949.
‘Yugoslavia’s break with Moscow offers an unprecedented opportunity. By keeping Tito alive, we demonstrate to other Eastern European leaders that escape from Stalin’s embrace is possible. Aid to Tito should be discreet, conditional and substantial — aimed not at converting him to the West but at proving that an independent communist state can survive.’

Identify two ways in which Source D is useful to a historian studying the wider impact of the Tito-Stalin split.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly developed points using content and provenance, reinforced by precise own knowledge.
Secure: Two clear points; uses content and either provenance or own knowledge; some development.
Developing: Two points but undeveloped, or one point fully and one weakly.
Emerging: One general point or surface description.

Indicative content:
• Content: Source D shows that the USA saw the Yugoslav break as a strategic opportunity to weaken Soviet control of the bloc as a whole — useful evidence that the impact of the split went well beyond Yugoslavia.
• Content: the policy of ‘discreet, conditional and substantial’ aid reveals US thinking that public friendship would be counter-productive.
• Provenance: a National Security Council report from 1949 is a high-level internal US policy document — close to the genuine American calculation of the period.
• Own knowledge: this matches the historical record — the USA quietly provided food and credits to Yugoslavia from 1949; later thinking on Hungary in 1956 echoed the same idea of national communism.
• Limitation worth noting: an internal report is one moment in a wider debate; it cannot show whether US officials maintained the ‘discreet’ line in practice.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source E.

Source E: An extract from a 1950 article in the Yugoslav newspaper Borba, defending the new Yugoslav line of independent socialism.
‘Comecon offers eastern Europe planning without choice, prices set in Moscow, and a single road to socialism. Yugoslavia has chosen another road. Workers in our factories make decisions through workers’ councils, our trade is open to East and West alike, and our diplomacy serves Yugoslav interests, not foreign ones.’

Secure: Identifies two relevant ways from the source, with brief support.
Developing: Identifies one clear way; second point vague or repeats the first.
Emerging: General comment about the source without identifying specific ways.

Indicative content:
• Yugoslavia uses workers’ councils to make factory decisions, rather than central planning from above.
• Yugoslav trade is open to East and West, not restricted to the Soviet bloc.
• Yugoslav diplomacy serves Yugoslav interests, not foreign ones.
• Yugoslavia rejects the ‘single road to socialism’ that the source attributes to Comecon.

lessons.title: The Berlin Blockade, Airlift and the Birth of NATO
lessons.description: Why Berlin became the first Cold War flashpoint and how the airlift led to NATO and divided Germany.
lessons.content_html:
Why Berlin Was the Pressure Point

Berlin in 1948 was a strange place. The city sat 160 kilometres inside the Soviet zone of occupation, but Berlin itself was divided into four sectors run by the Soviets, Americans, British and French. Western access depended on three air corridors agreed in 1945, plus road, rail and canal routes that had no comparable treaty cover. Stalin had a city the West needed but could not easily reach. Truman had a half-city full of West Berliners who increasingly rejected the Soviet model. The fuse was lit when the Western powers acted on the economy.

Key Fact

The Berlin Blockade ran from 24 June 1948 to 12 May 1949. Stalin closed all road, rail and canal access into West Berlin in response to the introduction of a new Western currency. The West responded with the Berlin Airlift — flying supplies into Tempelhof, Gatow and Tegel airports for nearly eleven months.

The Currency Trigger

By spring 1948 the Western occupiers had decided to merge their three zones economically and introduce a new, stable currency — the Deutsche Mark. The currency was launched in the Western zones on 20 June 1948. Three days later it was extended to the Western sectors of Berlin. Stalin saw this as a hostile act: a working economy in West Germany was the foundation of a future West German state, and a working economy in West Berlin would magnetise East Germans toward the Western system. He retaliated with a complete blockade.

From midnight on 24 June 1948, all road, rail and canal traffic into West Berlin was stopped. Electricity from the East was cut. The Berlin Blockade left a city of about 2.5 million people in the Western sectors with roughly six weeks of food and fuel stockpiled. Stalin’s assumption was simple: faced with a choice between abandoning Berlin or risking war, the West would abandon Berlin.

The Airlift

Truman refused both options. Direct military force could trigger a third world war; abandoning Berlin would gut Western credibility across Europe. Instead, the USA, Britain and France used the air corridors. The Berlin Airlift began on 26 June. At its peak in spring 1949, a transport aircraft was landing in West Berlin every ninety seconds, around the clock. Over 277,000 flights delivered roughly 2.3 million tonnes of food, coal and supplies. Coal was the surprising bulk — Berlin in winter could not survive on food alone.

The cost was real. Around 79 airmen died in crashes during the airlift, and the operation strained Western air capacity. But the political message was sharper than the cost. The Soviets had assumed the West would not undertake an airlift at scale; the West had done so. By the spring of 1949 it was clear that Berliners were not starving and that Soviet pressure had failed. On 12 May 1949 Stalin lifted the blockade. The airlift continued for another four months, building stockpiles in case Stalin tried again.

Soviet fighters could have shot down American transport aircraft over the corridors at any point during the airlift. They did not. The reason was the bomb. The USA still had the only working atomic weapons in the world and a small but functional fleet of B-29 bombers based in Britain. Stalin calculated that shooting down a US transport would risk a war he could not yet win. The airlift therefore worked because of a balance: the West would not invade with ground forces, and the Soviets would not engage in the air. This was the first practical lesson of the Cold War — both sides learned to push, but to stop short of the line that would trigger nuclear retaliation.

The Birth of NATO

The blockade convinced Western governments that the postwar arrangements were not enough. In Washington, London and Paris, planners agreed that Western Europe could not be defended by ad hoc coordination. On 4 April 1949 — while the airlift still ran — twelve countries signed the North Atlantic Treaty in Washington. The signatories were the USA, Canada, Britain, France, Italy, Belgium, the Netherlands, Luxembourg, Norway, Denmark, Iceland and Portugal. Article 5 of the treaty committed each member to treat an armed attack on any one as an attack on all.

The North Atlantic Treaty Organization — NATO — was the first peacetime US military alliance with European powers. For the USA it formalised the doctrine of containment with a defence guarantee. For Western Europe it brought American troops, air bases and (after 1951) the integrated command system run from SHAPE in Paris. For Stalin, NATO confirmed what Cominform had argued in 1947: the West was not just a political bloc but a military one. The Soviet response — the Warsaw Pact — would follow in 1955, after West Germany joined NATO.

The blockade settled the German question by accident. As long as the Allies treated Germany as a single occupied country with four zones, formal partition was avoided. Once Stalin had tried to starve out the Western sectors, no Western leader would trust the Soviet zone in any joint arrangement. On 23 May 1949, eleven days after the blockade ended, the three Western zones became the Federal Republic of Germany (West Germany), with its capital at Bonn. On 7 October 1949 the Soviet zone became the German Democratic Republic (East Germany), with its capital at East Berlin. The four-zone Germany of Yalta and Potsdam was gone — replaced by two German states tied to opposing alliances.

Key Fact

NATO was founded by twelve countries in Washington on 4 April 1949. Article 5 commits each member to treat an attack on one as an attack on all. The Federal Republic of Germany (West Germany) was created on 23 May 1949 and the German Democratic Republic (East Germany) on 7 October 1949 — the four-zone Germany was permanently divided.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For a 16-mark Source-Based Essay, plan two source paragraphs and a final paragraph that reaches a clear judgement. Each source paragraph should integrate a content point, a provenance point and one piece of own knowledge. The judgement paragraph weighs the proposition against an alternative explanation. The strongest answers do not just ‘use’ the sources — they show how each source helps or limits the case for the claim in the question.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Berlin Blockade, June 1948 to May 1949, began with the introduction of the Deutsche Mark in the Western sectors and was Stalin’s attempt to force the West out of West Berlin without using force.
  • The Berlin Airlift — 277,000 flights, 2.3 million tonnes — defeated the blockade by demonstrating that the West would supply Berlin under the bomb’s protection without firing on Soviet forces.
  • NATO, founded on 4 April 1949 by twelve countries, formalised the West’s commitment to collective defence under Article 5; West and East Germany were created later the same year, making the division of Germany permanent.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source A.

Source A: An extract from a memorandum by General Lucius Clay, US Military Governor in Germany, sent to Washington on 28 June 1948, four days into the Berlin Blockade.
‘If we abandon Berlin we shall lose all of western Europe within months. Berlin is small and isolated, but the principle on which it stands is the principle on which our entire policy in Europe rests. We must supply the city by air for as long as the airlift lasts; if we cannot, we should consider an armed convoy and accept the risk of war.’

Source B: An extract from a Soviet Military Administration statement issued in East Berlin on 30 June 1948.
‘The technical disturbances on rail and road routes into Berlin are the consequence of the unilateral currency reform forced upon the city by the Western powers. The Soviet Union cannot accept being asked to accept Western banknotes in our zone. Once the currency question is settled, normal traffic will resume.’

Write an essay on the question: ‘The Soviet Union was the main cause of the Berlin Blockade in 1948.’ Using Sources A and B and your own knowledge, evaluate the claim.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained argument addressing the specific claim; integrates content, provenance and own knowledge from both sources; reaches a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with relevant use of both sources; judgement reached and supported.
Developing: Some argument with reference to both sources, but use of provenance or own knowledge limited; judgement may be partial.
Emerging: Describes the sources or covers events without engaging with the specific claim.

Indicative content:
Supporting the claim:
• Source A frames the blockade as a Soviet attempt to force the West out of Berlin, with abandonment seen as catastrophic.
• Provenance: Clay was the US Military Governor with daily contact on the ground, useful as informed Western judgement.
• Own knowledge: Stalin closed road, rail and canal access from 24 June 1948; the blockade was a unilateral Soviet decision.
Challenging the claim:
• Source B places the blockade in the context of the Western currency reform, framing the closure as a technical response.
• Provenance: an official Soviet statement designed to put the West on the defensive — partial but useful for revealing how Moscow framed its actions.
• Own knowledge: the introduction of the Deutsche Mark in the Western zones on 20 June and in Western Berlin on 23 June was a direct trigger; Stalin’s reaction was extreme but not unprovoked.
Judgement: the USSR carried out the blockade and chose the maximum response, so was the proximate cause — but the deeper cause was the structural disagreement over Germany’s future, in which Western currency reform played a major part.

practice_questions.text: Construct a chronological explanation of how the Berlin Blockade led to the founding of NATO between June 1948 and April 1949.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A clear analytical narrative linking three or more events as a chain of cause and consequence; uses precise factual detail; arrives at the founding of NATO through a substantiated sequence.
Secure: A clear sequence of three or more linked events with some causal connectives and accurate detail.
Developing: Some relevant events listed in roughly the right order; causal links partial or implicit.
Emerging: A thin or muddled chronology with little linking between events.

Indicative content:
• 20–23 June 1948: introduction of the Deutsche Mark in the Western zones and Western Berlin triggered the Soviet response.
• 24 June 1948: Stalin imposed a full blockade of West Berlin.
• 26 June 1948: the airlift began; over the following months it scaled up to a delivery every ninety seconds at peak.
• Autumn 1948: Western governments concluded that ad hoc coordination was inadequate and began negotiating a treaty.
• 4 April 1949: twelve countries signed the North Atlantic Treaty in Washington, before the blockade had even ended.
• 12 May 1949: Stalin lifted the blockade, leaving NATO in place as the lasting institutional consequence.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source C.

Source C: An extract from a speech by US Secretary of State Dean Acheson at the signing of the North Atlantic Treaty, Washington, 4 April 1949.
‘This treaty does not begin a war and does not seek one. It declares that twelve democratic nations stand together to deter aggression. The events of the past year have shown what an unwillingness to stand together can cost — the Berlin Blockade is the latest reminder. We have learned the lesson, and we mean to act on it.’

Using Source C, identify two reasons Acheson gives for the founding of NATO.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies two clearly distinct reasons drawn precisely from the source, supported by short embedded references.
Secure: Identifies two relevant reasons from the source, with brief support.
Developing: Identifies one clear reason; second point vague or repeats the first.
Emerging: General comment about the source without identifying specific reasons.

Indicative content:
• Twelve democratic nations are standing together to deter aggression.
• The Berlin Blockade has shown the cost of not standing together.
• The treaty is defensive (it ‘does not seek’ war) and aimed at deterrence.
• The lesson of the past year is now driving institutional change.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source D.

Source D: An extract from a Pravda editorial, Moscow, 8 April 1949, four days after the North Atlantic Treaty was signed.
‘The North Atlantic alliance is presented as a defensive arrangement, but its essence is offensive. Twelve countries have placed themselves under the leadership of the United States and made the rebuilding of West Germany the cornerstone of their plans. The Soviet government can only conclude that war preparations have begun and must defend itself accordingly.’

Identify two ways in which Source D is useful to a historian studying Soviet reactions to the founding of NATO.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly developed points using content and provenance, reinforced by precise own knowledge.
Secure: Two clear points; uses content and either provenance or own knowledge; some development.
Developing: Two points but undeveloped, or one point fully and one weakly.
Emerging: One general point or surface description.

Indicative content:
• Content: the editorial reveals that Moscow framed NATO as offensive rather than defensive — useful evidence of how Soviet leaders justified their own military buildup.
• Content: the focus on the rebuilding of West Germany shows that Soviet anxiety about NATO was tied directly to the German question.
• Provenance: Pravda was the official Soviet Communist Party newspaper, so the editorial line is the government line — useful for capturing the public Soviet response in the days after the signing.
• Own knowledge: this matches later events — the West German Federal Republic was founded in May 1949; the Warsaw Pact would be founded in 1955 after West Germany joined NATO.
• Limitation worth noting: a public editorial reflects the line for foreign and domestic audiences, not necessarily the private Soviet calculation in the Politburo.

practice_questions.text: Construct a chronological explanation of how the Berlin Airlift broke the Soviet Blockade between June 1948 and May 1949.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analytical narrative with three or more linked events showing causation; precise dates and details; arrives at the lifting of the blockade through a substantiated chain.
Secure: Three or more linked events; some causal connectives; mostly accurate.
Developing: Events listed roughly in order; causal links partial.
Emerging: Thin chronology, weak linkage.

Indicative content:
• 24 June 1948: the Soviet blockade closed road, rail and canal access into West Berlin, leaving roughly six weeks of stockpiled food.

• Autumn 1948: the operation scaled up; Tegel airport was built in West Berlin in a few weeks to add a third runway.
• Winter 1948–49: coal was the largest cargo, sustaining heating and electricity through Berlin’s coldest months.
• Spring 1949: a transport landed every ninety seconds at peak; West Berliners were not starving and Soviet pressure was failing.
• 12 May 1949: Stalin lifted the blockade; the airlift continued until September to build stockpiles.

practice_questions.text:
Study Source E.

Source E: An extract from a private letter from Ernst Reuter, Mayor of West Berlin, to a friend abroad in November 1948.
‘The streets are cold and the lights flicker, but Berliners do not waver. They have understood that the airlift is more than coal and flour; it is a vote on whether free Europe still exists. Whatever happens in Washington, Moscow will not break us by hunger.’

Using Source E, identify two reasons Reuter gives for thinking Berliners would hold out against the blockade.

Secure: Identifies two relevant reasons from the source, with brief support.
Developing: Identifies one clear reason; second point vague or repeats the first.
Emerging: General comment about the source without identifying specific reasons.

Indicative content:
• Berliners see the airlift as a ‘vote on whether free Europe still exists’ — symbolic stake.
• They understand the airlift is ‘more than coal and flour’ — political meaning beyond physical supplies.
• Berliners do not waver despite cold and flickering lights — visible commitment.
• Reuter is confident Moscow ‘will not break us by hunger’.
